ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description: On the left side of the figure is a DC capacitor C, connected to a three-phase voltage source converter labeled three phase voltage source converter; the AC side of the converter is connected through a reactor to the AC grid on the right. Reasoning: The initial steady state is δ = 0, and losses and harmonics are ignored, so the steady-state real power exchange is zero. If the DC capacitor voltage is to be raised slowly, active power must be input from the AC grid into the converter, so that energy is stored in the capacitor. When transmitting active power through a series reactor, the converter-side voltage phase needs to lag the grid voltage; because the grid phase angle is fixed at 0, this corresponds to adjusting δ to a negative value. After the capacitor voltage rises to the new steady-state value, it is no longer necessary to continue inputting active power, so δ should be restored to the original 0.

method.method_draft: First identify from the image that the converter is tied to the grid through a reactor, with the grid angle fixed at 0 and the converter angle controlled by δ. The text says the initial steady state has δ=0 and asks how to raise the DC capacitor voltage slowly. Since increasing capacitor voltage requires importing real power from the AC side into the converter, choose δ so the converter voltage lags the grid voltage. With the grid at angle 0, that means set δ negative for the charging interval. Once Vdc reaches the new steady value, return δ to 0 so the lossless steady-state real power exchange goes back to zero.

method.method_draft: Read the diagram to model the converter and grid as two sinusoidal voltage sources separated by a reactor. From the text, start at δ=0 and Vdc0. Write the real-power transfer across the reactor as Pconv→ac = (Ei E/X) sin δ.
